messages.subject: R square
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am running a model with sample (23), the curious thing is that when I run the model with lm it has a high R2 = .4, but when I run it with blavaan it has a much lower R2 = .1

Even when I try more informative priors

Any idea why the R2 are so different?

Thanks

Hi Ed

The argument fixed.x made no difference in either blavaan or lavaan. In blavaan was always around .11

Lavaan was actually similar to lm R2=.43

Any idea why blavaan is so different?

Thanks

>

messages.subject: Re: R square
messages.body_plain:
I looked at some other regression examples, and the blavaan R2 matches lavaan pretty closely. Also, blavaan gets its R2 values by calling lavaan code, so I'm not convinced there is a bug here.

In your case, I think the difference comes from the estimated variance of BMD, which is .062 for blavaan and .010 for lavaan. In other words, blavaan thinks that BMD has more variance to explain, so the percentage of explained variance is lower. I am guessing that this can be traced back to the prior on the variance of BMD. The default is gamma(1,.5), which maybe isn't so great for such small variances. You might look at prior sensitivity here.

Ed

Hi all

This Fall the Stats Camp is coming to California, with 3 day courses. We have a register now, pay later option so folks can reserve a seat. The URL for the fall camp is: https://www.statscamp.org/fall-camp/ <https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.statscamp.org_fall-2Dcamp_&d=DwMFAg&c=S1d2Gs1Y1NQV8Lx35_Qi5FnTH2uYWyh_OhOS94IqYCo&r=YjdBtnf8LkLLcph3uDej4yPlM-OYnqhJIOLDc94Bmvr-FMi1GhVi50uqK3ALNJIo&m=5FHIhz8dRc8VyLhxGbFVr9zrPf9RSO07c4CoBcTBMIw&s=0Lehdr3YakD8wvWbiKA6Z4eK9-IXK-iMnEtsA7Tes7M&e=>

Statistics Course Offerings in Orange County:

Applied Latent Class Analysis (LCA) Course

– Instructor, Katherine Masyn, Ph.D.

This is an intermediate 3-day course introducing latent class analysis with categorical, cross-sectional data using Mplus.

Bayesian Data Analysis Course

– Instructor, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal, Ph.D.

An introductory 3-day course about Bayesian Data Analysis, focus on the differences to the frequentist approach, and application of several models

Item Response Theory (IRT) Course

Psychometrics Course

This is an introductory 3-day course in the foundations of psychometrics. Participants should be proficient specific to the material covered in a two-semester graduate-level social science statistics course sequence.

messages.subject: Re: probelm whe covariance is fix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mauricio,

The "leading minor of order 6" thing might indeed be a bug (using cp="fa"). I will have to check it out.

I think the "invalid parent values" thing (using cp="srs") indicates that the initial values are bad (maybe leading to a correlation greater than 1 or variance less than 0). I played with a similar example using HolzingerSwineford1939 (that name is going to give me carpal tunnel), and even lavaan sometimes had problems with starting values there. Also, when I changed the fixed covariance to something closer to 0 (say, .05 instead of 1), the model worked under cp="srs". So I would advise to manually specify your initial values for now (there is an example in the blavaan paper of how to do this).

I will also look at smarter initial value specification here. Right now, I don't think the initial values are influenced by other parameter constraints, which is presumably what caused problems here.

Ed

messages.subject: Re: probelm whe covariance is fix
messages.body_plain:
Mauricio,

I recalled a simpler issue that might help you here. Fixing covariance parameters separately from the variances is a funny thing, because covariances are influenced by variances. When I first coded this stuff, I allowed the user to only fix the correlation related to the covariance, instead of the covariance itself. This is because the correlation can be specified separately from the variances.

In your example, blavaan sees the fixed "1" and is setting the xi1~~xi2 correlation to 1. This would explain the problems. (If you have a good argument for why you need to fix the covariance instead, I could be convinced.)

I also found another bug related to this and fixed it in the development version.

One other minor thing: blavaan currently cannot fully handle a prior parameter involving arithmetic (like 1/2.5 in your t distributions). The model will be estimated correctly, but some posthoc marginal likelihood computations fail. Better to directly specify the value "0.4".

Ed

Hi Ed

Fixing the correlation make sense, and is the intention of this constraint. This is a model for a simulation, the constraint is the misspecification, we found another way to specify the same misspecification.

I did noticed in my tests that the marginal LL wasnt calculated, will change to those priors

Thanks

On Wednesday, August 16, 2017 at 3:28:02 PM UTC-5, Ed Merkle wrote:

> Mauricio,
>
> I recalled a simpler issue that might help you here. Fixing covariance parameters separately from the variances is a funny thing, because covariances are influenced by variances. When I first coded this stuff, I allowed the user to only fix the correlation related to the covariance, instead of the covariance itself. This is because the correlation can be specified separately from the variances.
>
> In your example, blavaan sees the fixed "1" and is setting the xi1~~xi2 correlation to 1. This would explain the problems. (If you have a good argument for why you need to fix the covariance instead, I could be convinced.)
>
> I also found another bug related to this and fixed it in the development version.
>
> One other minor thing: blavaan currently cannot fully handle a prior parameter involving arithmetic (like 1/2.5 in your t distributions). The model will be estimated correctly, but some posthoc marginal likelihood computations fail. Better to directly specify the value "0.4".
>
> Ed
>

> On Tue, Aug 15, 2017 at 9:17 PM, Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Hi Mauricio,
> >
> > The "leading minor of order 6" thing might indeed be a bug (using cp="fa"). I will have to check it out.
> >
> > I think the "invalid parent values" thing (using cp="srs") indicates that the initial values are bad (maybe leading to a correlation greater than 1 or variance less than 0). I played with a similar example using HolzingerSwineford1939 (that name is going to give me carpal tunnel), and even lavaan sometimes had problems with starting values there. Also, when I changed the fixed covariance to something closer to 0 (say, .05 instead of 1), the model worked under cp="srs". So I would advise to manually specify your initial values for now (there is an example in the blavaan paper of how to do this).
> >
> > I will also look at smarter initial value specification here. Right now, I don't think the initial values are influenced by other parameter constraints, which is presumably what caused problems here.
> >
> > Ed
> >
> >
